questions.question: Q1. What is the biggest difference between how structured light and LiDAR scan a room?

answers.a: LiDAR uses visible light, while structured light uses infrared.
answers.b: LiDAR measures depth one point at a time by timing laser pulses, while structured light projects a pattern over the whole scene and decodes depth simultaneously based on how the pattern bends.
answers.c: Structured light only works on flat surfaces.
answers.d: LiDAR requires two sensors, but structured light only needs one.

explanations.a: Not quite! The difference isn't about the colour of the light. Both can use various wavelengths. The real difference is in how they gather data.
explanations.b: Spot on! LiDAR measures one point at a time by timing how long a laser takes to bounce back. Structured light throws a patterned 'net' over the whole scene; the camera captures the entire distorted pattern at once, letting us calculate the height of every point simultaneously. Learn more about structured light
explanations.c: Incorrect. Structured light is fantastic at measuring complex, curvy, and bumpy surfaces!
explanations.d: Incorrect. A structured light setup actually requires two devices (a projector and a camera), whereas a LiDAR scanner is often an integrated single unit.

questions.question: Q2. In a fringe projection system, what exactly is the 'phase' (φ) at a specific pixel?

answers.a: The average brightness of that pixel.
answers.b: Your exact position within one black-and-white cycle of the wavy pattern, which tells us the height of the object at that spot.
answers.c: The specific color of the light hitting the object.
answers.d: The angle of the camera sensor.

explanations.a: Nope, average brightness is the 'DC term' (A), not the phase. Phase is what actually encodes the 3D shape!
explanations.b: Exactly! Phase tells you where you are within a single wave cycle (from 0 to 2π). When the surface height changes, the wave physically shifts sideways from the camera's perspective. That shift changes the phase, and we use that phase to calculate height!
explanations.c: Incorrect. Structured light usually uses simple white or single-color light. The depth secret is hidden in the geometry of the stripes, not their color.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The angle of the camera is a fixed physical setup parameter (baseline angle α), not the phase.

questions.question: Q3. Why do we need to project multiple shifted fringe images instead of just snapping one picture?

answers.a: It just makes the computer process it faster.
answers.b: A single image can't tell if a dark spot is a shadow on the object or the dark part of the projected stripe. Multiple images give us enough mathematical clues to figure it out.
answers.c: Cameras aren't sensitive enough to capture a single image.
answers.d: We don't; one image is always enough.

explanations.a: Incorrect. Taking multiple images actually slows down the capture process, but it's mathematically necessary!
explanations.b: Correct! If you only take one picture, you have one equation but three unknowns (ambient light, fringe contrast, and phase). By shifting the pattern and taking at least 3 pictures, we get enough equations to separate the object's actual color from the phase (the height data).
explanations.c: Incorrect. Even with a perfect, noise-free camera, you physically cannot extract phase from a single static image without making assumptions.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A single image leaves the math 'underdetermined'-you can't solve it!

questions.question: Q4. In the math that drives this (I = A + B × cos(φ + shift)), what does 'B' represent?

answers.a: The distance between the camera and projector.
answers.b: The fringe contrast-how strongly the stripes stand out against the background.
answers.c: The total number of images taken.
answers.d: Whether the pixel is perfectly black or perfectly white.

explanations.a: Incorrect. The baseline distance is a completely different parameter related to triangulation.
explanations.b: Spot on! 'B' is the modulation amplitude-basically, how punchy and visible the stripes are. If B is high, the stripes are clear and we get great 3D data. If B is low, the stripes are washed out and the math fails.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The number of images is 'N', not 'B'.
explanations.d: Incorrect. These are smooth, continuous cosine waves, not harsh binary black-and-white pixels.

questions.question: Q5. If we use the standard four-step phase shifting formula, how many separate photos do we need to take?

explanations.a: Incorrect. One photo doesn't give us enough math equations.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Two photos still leaves us short.
explanations.c: Almost! While 3 is the absolute mathematical minimum for phase shifting, the four-step formula specifically requires 4.
explanations.d: Exactly! The four-step formula requires four distinct photos, each with the projector pattern shifted by exactly a quarter of a cycle (0, π/2, π, and 3π/2). More on phase shifting

questions.question: Q6. What does 'phase wrapping' look like in a structured light measurement?

answers.a: Wrapping a printed calibration pattern around a cylinder.
answers.b: A weird visual glitch where the 3D surface suddenly drops off like a cliff because the math hit its π limit and reset to -π.
answers.c: A protective lens cover for the projector.
answers.d: Compressing the image files to save space.

explanations.a: Incorrect. It's a mathematical glitch, not a physical action.
explanations.b: Correct! Because the arctan function can only spit out values between -π and +π, anything taller than that 'wraps' around, creating ugly sawtooth cliffs in your 3D model. We have to 'unwrap' these jumps later in software to get the true height.
explanations.c: Incorrect. It has nothing to do with hardware casing.
explanations.d: Incorrect. It's a fundamental math constraint, not a data compression trick.

questions.question: Q7. Why is the modulation ratio (M = B / A) such a big deal for scan quality?

answers.a: It's the magnification of the lens-higher means bigger stripes.
answers.b: It's the signal-to-noise ratio. If M is low, the stripes are too faint to see against the background, and the math fails.
answers.c: It tells you how many stripes fit on the screen.
answers.d: It measures how shiny the object is.

explanations.a: Incorrect. It has nothing to do with optical magnification.
explanations.b: Spot on! M measures how strongly the stripes stand out. If you have a ton of ambient light (high A) but dim stripes (low B), M drops near zero. The camera just sees a washed-out blur, and your 3D scan is ruined.
explanations.c: Incorrect. That's fringe frequency, not modulation ratio.
explanations.d: Incorrect. While shininess affects B, M is a ratio of fringe contrast to background light, not a direct material property.

questions.question: Q8. How does widening the angle (α) between the projector and camera affect your scan?

answers.a: It makes the system less sensitive to height changes.
answers.b: It makes the system MORE sensitive to height changes-small bumps become much more obvious to the camera.
answers.c: It doesn't affect height sensitivity at all.
answers.d: It only changes how wide an area you can scan.

explanations.a: Incorrect. Actually, a wider angle increases sensitivity!
explanations.b: Correct! Think of it like shining a flashlight across a textured wall from an angle-the shadows and distortions get much longer and more exaggerated. A wider angle α means the same tiny bump causes a much bigger phase shift, giving you better depth resolution.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The angle α is a core part of the triangulation math.
explanations.d: Incorrect. While it does change the overlapping field of view, its primary mathematical effect is on depth sensitivity.

questions.question: Q9. Why do professionals usually scan in a dark room?

answers.a: To stop the projector from overheating.
answers.b: Because ambient room light acts like visual noise, washing out the projected stripes and destroying the contrast needed for the math.
answers.c: It just makes the colors on the 3D model look prettier.
answers.d: To keep the stripes from rotating.

explanations.a: Incorrect. Heat management is handled by fans, not room lighting.
explanations.b: Exactly! Ambient light raises the background intensity (A) without adding to the fringe strength (B). This plummets your modulation ratio (M = B/A). If the stripes wash out, the phase math returns pure garbage.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Ambient light ruins the *geometry* of the scan, not just the color.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Light doesn't cause optical rotation.

questions.question: Q10. What is the annoying trade-off when you use super thin stripes (high frequency)?

answers.a: You have to buy a more expensive projector.
answers.b: You get amazing detail on small bumps, but tall or steep objects cause the math to 'wrap' and fail.
answers.c: There is no trade-off; thinner is always better.
answers.d: It takes longer for the computer to process.

explanations.a: Incorrect. While good projectors cost more, the trade-off is a law of physics, not economics.
explanations.b: Correct! Thin stripes give you insane resolution for microscopic details. But because the stripes are so close together, a steep cliff on the object will make neighboring stripes overlap from the camera's perspective. This confuses the unwrapping algorithm and creates massive errors.
explanations.c: Incorrect. If thinner was always better, everyone would just project microscopic stripes. The wrapping problem prevents this.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The math takes the same amount of time regardless of how wide the stripes are.
